Dyson: Vacuum Cleaner or Alien Mega-Structure?

When you hear “Dyson,” what pops into your head? A brand of vacuum cleaner? Or cutting-edge technology developed by an extraterrestrial civilization—a mega-structure built around a star to harvest its energy?

The second option, let’s admit, is a lot more exciting—and today, it’s Dyson spheres that scientists are talking about again. The idea was first proposed in 1960 by physicist Freeman Dyson as a way to detect alien presence in the light we receive from distant stars.

The Great Dyson Sphere Hunt: TESS and James Webb Join Forces

Up till now, all attempts at detection have failed. But astronomers now have a dazzling new tool: the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) with its piercing infrared vision.

Why infrared? Think about it: a lightbulb or your laptop, they both give off heat. A technology advanced enough to exploit the energy of a star—and on such a massive scale—would naturally emit even more. The laws of thermodynamics are, well, pretty ruthless.

The Search for Extra Heat: A Galactic Game of Hide and Seek

We know the James Webb Space Telescope is able to detect certain chemical signatures in the atmosphere of a handful of exoplanets—potential biosignatures, though probably ambiguous for decades to come. But it’s a different story with technosignatures like those from Dyson spheres. Could JWST have already spotted something? There’s always hope…

Standing by and ready, JWST should be able to pick up this excess thermal radiation in the mid-infrared. So the researchers in Project Hephaistos, led by astrophysicist Erik Zackrisson at Uppsala University in Sweden, combed through archives covering some five million stars in the Milky Way. Their hope? To find at least one star with more mid-infrared light than it should emit under normal circumstances.

All ideas are fair game for finding traces of alien life—including searching for a technosignature produced by an advanced civilization. In fact, researchers have spotted potential hints of such signatures around several dozen stars.

But plot twist! As soon as the first images came through, astronomers were greeted by the unexpected: a second source right next to the stars—what they called candidate D and candidate E. It wasn’t the stars themselves giving off the suspicious (or exciting, depending on your mood) infrared radiation. The spectral data confirmed it.

Dyson Spheres, Freeman Dyson, and an Unexpected Ending

So, what was actually hiding behind candidate D? A galaxy, heated by its supermassive black hole stoking up enormous clouds of dust. As for candidate E, it turns out it’s likely a galaxy producing stars at a breathtaking pace. Both are types of galaxies that naturally emit the infrared radiation scientists were hoping to pin on Dyson spheres.

Let’s stay positive. This story, even if it didn’t confirm alien mega-structures, helped astronomers uncover two interesting galaxies that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. Plus, it pushed researchers to develop new techniques to tease apart overlapping light sources—a handy skill for cosmic detective work.

A new study may rule out the two most promising candidates so far, but it’s sharpening the tools needed to distinguish a genuine artificial signal from simple galactic “noise.” With upcoming JWST campaigns and future infrared surveys, the hunt for Dyson spheres—and technosignatures more broadly—is definitively entering a more mature phase. Maybe next time, the excess infrared emission really will be extraterrestrial?
